hub.name: Fractions, one piece at a time

questions.prompt: In 3/5, which number tells you how many equal parts make the whole?
questions.explanation: The denominator, five, names the size of the parts.
Zero selected sixths means none of the whole is selected.

questions.prompt: How much is 7/7 of a whole?
questions.explanation: All seven of the seven equal parts are present.

title: Numerator and denominator: how to read a fraction
practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.html:
A strip is divided into five equal parts. Three parts are shaded. Say “three fifths” and write 3/5. The slash separates two jobs: counting selected parts and naming their size.

The bottom number, five, is the denominator. It tells you the whole was divided into five equal parts. The top number, three, is the numerator. It tells you three of those parts are selected.
sections.title: Read the picture first

sections.html:
Draw a strip with five equal parts. Shade one part at a time, writing 1/5, 2/5 and so on beside it. Each step adds another fifth; the pieces stay the same size.

Now select one part and change the denominator. One half, one third and one fifth all have a numerator of one, but the selected pieces have different sizes. Their names tell you what sort of piece is being counted.
sections.title: Try it yourself

sections.html:
Zero fifths, written 0/5, means none of the five parts is selected. Five fifths, written 5/5, means every part is selected, so you have one whole.

A denominator cannot be zero in these fractions. “Divide the whole into zero equal parts” does not give a usable size of piece. One whole can be written as 1/1; splitting it into smaller pieces gives halves, thirds and so on.
sections.title: Nothing and everything

sections.html:
Three fifths does not mean three objects plus five objects. It means three pieces, each one fifth of a whole. Saying the fraction aloud can help you remember that relationship.

Try drawing seven equal boxes in a row and shading two. The fraction is 2/7 even if you separate the shaded boxes. Their positions do not change how many equal parts are selected.
sections.title: Avoid a tempting shortcut

description: The bottom number names the pieces. The top number counts how many of them you have.
